Kaya toast is a staple of[NL]Singaporean cuisine that[NL]I fell in love with during my[NL]first visit there, and also where[NL]I get my username from.[NL][NL]This recipe is based on a recipe[NL]my friends and I used to make,[NL]and it is an authentic method.[NL][NL]The recipe below is only for[NL]the kaya itself. For toast, you[NL]will often see it served[NL]at Singaporean coffee shops,[NL]or kopitiams, with butter[NL]on soft white bread. When[NL]I make at home, I usually[NL]skip the butter and just[NL]slather this on my bread.[NL][NL]Pandan leaves, sometimes[NL]called screwpine leaves,[NL]can usually be found in[NL]Southeast Asian food stores.[NL]In the western world,[NL]you will likely find it in[NL]the frozen section,[NL]since pandan does not[NL]typically grow in the[NL]western hemisphere.[NL][NL]Core Ingredients:[NL][NL]1 cup/200g  of coconut milk[NL]1 cup/200g granulated sugar [NL](I usually cut this, but would [NL]not go less than 1/2 cup)[NL]3 eggs[NL]3 egg yolks[NL]8 pandan leaves[NL][NL]Method:[NL][NL]In a small saucepot, mix[NL]together the coconut milk[NL]and 1 cup of sugar. Tie the[NL]8 pandan leaves into a knot[NL]and stir it into the saucepot,[NL]bringing to a boil over high heat.[NL]Throughout this process, keep[NL]the pandan leaves submerged[NL]as much as possible so that[NL]the leaves cook and soften.[NL][NL]When the milk has come to a boil,[NL]remove from heat and let the[NL]mixture steep for 10 minutes. [NL]Remove the pandan leaves from[NL]the milk, squeezing any excess[NL]liquid from the leaves into the[NL]milk. Be careful, as the leaves[NL]will be hot! Toss leaves after[NL]you wring them dry.[NL][NL]Separately, in a medium stainless[NL]steel mixing bowl, whisk together[NL]the eggs and yolks. Whisk in[NL]the coconut milk mixture to form[NL]a custard base.[NL][NL]Plce the stainless steel bowl over[NL]a medium pot of lightly simmering[NL]water. Gently cook the custard,[NL]stirring consstantly with a rupper[NL]spatula until the mixture thickens.[NL]This usually will take 15-20[NL]minutes, but could take longer[NL]depending on your setup.[NL]The final texture should have[NL]a thick custard consistency.[NL]Your spatula should leave[NL]a trail in the custard for[NL]10 seconds on the surface.[NL][NL]Immediately remove from the[NL]heat and strain into a medium[NL]bowl set over a larger bowl of[NL]ice water. Stir until the custard[NL]cools, then cover and refrigerate[NL]until needed. [NL][NL]This makes about 2 cups of[NL]coconut jam, or 400 grams.[NL]The jam generally keeps for[NL]1-2 weeks.
